0: Before training a model we often run into this problem:
1: I have a lot of raw material, product descriptions, operation manuals and business specifications, each in its own format, and the content is fairly scattered.
2: How do I put this data to use?
3: And if I train directly on domain or scenario data, will the finished model still be able to answer general knowledge questions?
4: So the key point is how we turn all the material into training data the model can use.
5: At the same time, cleaning, deduplicating and masking the data are essential. We may have distilled data, but it needs to be adapted to the result we want.
6: For instance, when training a model, if the self-awareness data has not been trained well, it may answer that it is the ChatGPT model, the Claude model and so on.
7: Data is the foundation of everything. This chapter starts from data sources and looks at how scattered material goes through synthesis, cleaning, deduplication and masking to become data you can hand to a model for training.
9: Collecting and annotating training data from scratch takes a lot of time and cost. For common tasks such as text classification, question answering and text generation, suitable public datasets can be found and added to training.
11: Text classification and inference: GLUE, SuperGLUE, CLUE, etc.;
12: Reading comprehension and question answering: SQuAD, CMRC, etc.;
14: Dialogue and instruction fine-tuning: Alpaca, ShareGPT, OpenOrca, etc.;
15: Multimodal tasks: COCO and other image-text datasets.

18: Open data is mainly used to supplement the model's general ability. If the model needs to learn a company's internal products, terminology, business rules and processes, the corresponding business data must be prepared.
20: Business data comes from an enterprise's actual business systems and business material and is closer to the scenario where the model will finally be used. General Q&A data lets the model learn a basic way of answering, while internal enterprise Q&A data can further let it learn product names, business terminology and handling rules.
22: Enterprise documents: product descriptions, operation manuals, business specifications, process documents, etc., from which product knowledge, business rules and operating procedures can be extracted;
23: Customer service records: historical user-customer service conversations, tickets and complaint records, usable to construct intent recognition, Q&A and dialogue data;
24: FAQ: questions and standard answers compiled by business staff, directly convertible into Q&A training data;
25: Expert cases: typical problems handled by business experts and their outcomes, usable to construct training data for complex business scenarios.
26: Business data generally cannot be used for model training directly. A business manual of tens of pages, for example, must first have its body text extracted from Word, PDF and similar files and then be organised into Q&A pairs, classification samples or instruction data according to the training task. Customer service records may also contain system messages, invalid conversations and duplicated content, which must be filtered and tidied first.
27: Business data may also contain sensitive content such as names, phone numbers, ID numbers and customer information. Before entering a training dataset it must be masked according to the enterprise's data security requirements, so that real sensitive information is not used directly for model training.
29: In real projects the data you have may not meet every training need. Some business types may have only a few samples, or the documents you have may contain knowledge but no Q&A data usable for training. In that case a large model can generate new training samples, an approach called data synthesis.
31: Instruction data synthesis: from an existing task or a few examples, have a large model generate new instructions and answers;
32: Q&A data synthesis: feed business documents and have the model generate questions and answers from them;
33: Classification data synthesis: specify the class labels and examples and have the model generate text for the corresponding classes;
34: Boundary data synthesis: generate similar samples for easily confused classes, to strengthen the model's ability to judge class boundaries.
35: For example, an enterprise has only a product operation manual and no Q&A data. The manual must first be split by chapter or paragraph, and the model used to generate several questions and answers from each paragraph. After checking the results, they are organised into Q&A training data.
36: Data synthesis reduces the work of writing training samples by hand and can fill in scenarios where the raw data is insufficient. But synthetic data cannot be used for training as soon as it is generated. A large model may produce wrong answers or duplicated samples, or invent products and business rules that do not exist, so quality checks are still needed.
38: The quality of synthetic data directly affects training. Before adding synthetic data to the training set, check whether the generated content is correct and filter out wrong, fabricated, duplicated and overly similar data.
40: If the synthetic data was generated from business documents, check whether the generated content agrees with the original.
41: For example, the original business document states:
42: A refund application must go through manual review, and the refund can only be made after the review passes.
43: The Q&A data the model generated:
44: Q: Does a refund require review?
45: A: Once the refund is submitted it is refunded automatically, with no manual review needed.
46: This answer conflicts with the business rule; used for training it could teach the model a wrong business process.

59: When a large model generates data in bulk it easily produces duplicated or highly similar samples. For example: “How do I change my login password?” and “How is the login password changed?” are worded differently but basically the same in content. Too many such samples lower the effective information in the dataset.
60: After synthetic data is generated you need to check for duplication and similarity between samples, filter out exactly duplicated data, limit the number of highly similar samples and keep representative ones. The concrete deduplication methods are covered in the next section.
62: Whether data comes from open datasets, enterprise business data or large-model synthesis, it must be processed uniformly before training. The usual steps are data collection, data cleaning, data deduplication and data masking.
64: Data collection means obtaining the needed data from different sources according to the training task and organising it uniformly.
65: Before collecting you must decide what data the training task needs. A classification task needs text and a class label, a Q&A task needs question and answer, and instruction fine-tuning needs an instruction and the corresponding answer. During collection keep only the data and fields relevant to the training task.
66: Data from different sources may have different structures. One dataset may use the fields question and answer, another may use query and response. After collection the field names and data structure must be unified to make later processing easier.
67: For data missing necessary information, the gap can be filled during collection: for example adding a class label to classification data, or compiling a reference answer for Q&A data.
69: Raw data may contain invalid or wrong content that must be cleaned before training.
70: Common processing includes: deleting blank data and invalid records, removing redundant HTML tags and special characters, unifying text encoding and format, and correcting obvious OCR errors.
71: Cleaning does not mean deleting all special content. Code, formulas, units and punctuation may themselves be part of the training content, so whether to keep them depends on the task.

77: After data collected from different sources is aggregated, content may be identical or similar. The same FAQ may appear at once in an open dataset, a product manual and a customer service knowledge base, and synthetic data may also resemble existing data. Too much duplicated data lowers the diversity of the training set and makes the model over-learn certain knowledge or ways of expressing it, so the data must be deduplicated uniformly before training.
78: By degree of duplication, deduplication can be split into exact deduplication and similarity deduplication:
79: Exact deduplication: judging whether two records are completely identical, which can be done by text matching or a hash value.
80: Similarity deduplication: judging whether two records, though worded differently, are highly close in content, detectable with methods such as MinHash, SimHash or vector similarity.
81: Different kinds of data need different deduplication rules. Taking an FAQ dataset as an example, you can combine the question and the answer into one complete piece of text and then judge whether different samples are duplicated or similar.

For detected similar data, decide whether to delete, merge or keep according to the similarity threshold and the business need, so that data with training value is not removed by mistake.
135: Enterprise business data may contain sensitive information such as names, phone numbers, ID numbers, addresses and account numbers. Before it enters a training dataset it must be masked according to data security requirements.
136: Masking requires first identifying the sensitive information in the data and then choosing the right handling by type of sensitive information.
138: Before masking you must determine which content in the data is sensitive. For text data, regular expressions or a sensitive-information detection model can be used.
140: Regular expressions match text according to predefined format rules and suit identifying information with a fixed format, such as mobile numbers, ID card numbers, bank card numbers and e-mail addresses. The code that uses a regular expression to identify sensitive information is as follows:
142: A regular expression gives you the content, type and position in the original text of the sensitive information, which you can then use for masking. Regular expressions rely mainly on format features and work well for information with a fixed structure. In practice you must write and test rules for the format of your business data. For information that needs context to be understood, such as names and addresses, a regular expression alone is hard pressed to identify reliably.
144: For information that needs semantic understanding, such as names, addresses and organisations, a sensitive-information detection model can be used.
145: For example, the open-source ZJUICSR/AIguard-pii-detection-fast is a model for Chinese personally identifiable information (PII) detection and can identify names, mobile numbers, ID card numbers, addresses, e-mail addresses and more.

148: In real business, regular expressions and sensitive-information detection models are often combined: regular expressions handle information with a fixed format quickly, such as mobile numbers and e-mail addresses, while the model handles information needing semantic understanding, such as names and addresses.
150: Once sensitive information is identified, choose the right handling according to the type of sensitive information and the training task.
153: Replacement swaps real sensitive information for other content. It can be fixed or random:
154: Fixed replacement: generate the replacement by a fixed rule, for example replacing the given name in a full name with “X”, so “Zhang San” becomes “Zhang X” and “Li Si” becomes “Li X”. Because the rule is fixed, the same information always gives the same result and no mapping has to be stored. The processing code is as follows:
155: Random replacement: pick fictitious information at random to replace the real information, such as replacing “Zhang San” with “Li Ming”. If the same “Zhang San” appears in several places, the replacement must stay consistent, otherwise data that belonged to one object could be replaced with different identities and the relations in the data would break. Random replacement therefore usually needs a mapping table: {"Zhang San":"Li Ming"}, so that the next time “Zhang San” appears “Li Ming” is used directly. The processing code is as follows:

160: Generalisation lowers the precision of information and reduces the ability to pin the data to a specific object. It is often used for continuous information such as addresses, ages and times.
162: Sensitive fields irrelevant to the training task can be deleted directly. If the training task only needs to learn the Q&A relation, names and mobile numbers can be removed.
163: In practice the masking method must be chosen together with the training task and the characteristics of the data. When the relations between different samples must be preserved, fixed replacement or random replacement with a mapping can be used; when part of the information's features must be kept, masking or generalisation can be used; and sensitive information irrelevant to the task can simply be deleted.
164: Different business scenarios have different data characteristics, so the concrete masking rules need adjusting to the actual need. The code in this section only illustrates the basic handling methods.
166: Once data processing is done, the data must also be organised into the format the training framework requires.
167: Instruction tuning is a common fine-tuning approach for large language models. The training data contains the user's instruction and the answer the model is expected to generate, teaching the model how to complete a task as instructed.
168: Different training frameworks may use different data fields. The common instruction data formats are mainly Alpaca, ShareGPT and Messages.
170: The Alpaca format is simple in structure and usually uses the three fields instruction, input and output; it suits single-turn instruction data.
171: Here: instruction is the task the model must perform; input is the input content needed to complete the task; output is the answer the model is expected to generate.
172: If the task itself needs no extra input, input can be empty.
174: This format has few fields and a clear structure, and suits single-turn tasks such as Q&A, classification and text generation.
176: Another common approach is to store the dialogue in messages, where each message has two main fields, role and content.
177: Here system sets the model's role, task requirement or answering rules, user is the user's input and assistant is the answer the model is expected to generate.
178: The Messages format also supports multi-turn dialogue: just keep adding user and assistant messages in the actual conversation order.
180: ShareGPT is one of the common dialogue data formats in open large-model training. It usually stores the whole conversation in conversations and distinguishes the user from the model with human and gpt.
181: The ShareGPT format can also store multi-turn dialogue:
183: The Alpaca, Messages and ShareGPT formats all essentially describe the model's input and expected output; only the way the fields are organised differs.
184: You can choose according to the task type and the training framework:
188: Organises data with instruction, input and output
191: Stores the dialogue in messages and distinguishes roles with role
194: Stores the dialogue in conversations and distinguishes roles with from
195: The formats can usually be converted into one another. One Alpaca record, for example, can be converted into a set of user and assistant messages, and human and gpt in ShareGPT can likewise be converted into user and assistant respectively. In practice you should first confirm the data format and model template the training framework supports and then organise the data accordingly.
